sections.title: Topics, Partitions and the Commit Log

blocks.text:
A topic is the name under which related records are published, such as `orders` or `payments`. But a topic is not where the data physically lives. If a topic were one long sequence on one machine, its size, its write rate and its read rate would all be limited by that single machine, and every consumer would have to read the same single stream. Kafka's answer is to split each topic into **partitions**. A partition is a small, self-contained, append-only log; a topic is a named group of them. This one design decision explains most of what you will observe in practice: how Kafka scales, what it promises about ordering, why consumer groups behave the way they do, and why adding partitions later is risky.

### The commit log

A **log**, in this sense, is not a text file full of debug messages. It is one of the oldest and simplest data structures in computing: a sequence of records that you can only append to at the end and read by position. Databases keep one internally (the write-ahead log, or commit log) so that they can recover after a crash. Kafka makes the log the product itself and calls each position an **offset**.

blocks.text:
Four properties of a partition do most of the work:

- **Append-only and immutable.** New records go at the end. A record is never modified in place; "updating" something means appending a newer record.
- **Sequential offsets.** The broker gives each record the next number (0, 1, 2, ...) as it is appended. Offsets are never reused, even after old records have been deleted. An offset only has meaning inside one partition: the triple (topic, partition, offset) identifies one record.
- **Read by position.** A consumer says "send me records starting at offset 42". The broker does not track which records have been delivered; the consumer remembers its own position. Records stay until retention removes them (by age or size), whether or not anybody has read them.
- **Sequential I/O.** Appending at the end and reading in order are both sequential access patterns, which disks, the operating system's page cache and networks handle best. The chapter on the storage engine shows how much of Kafka's speed comes from this.

Because nothing is removed when it is read, one log can serve many independent readers. The payment service, an analytics job and a brand new search indexer can all read `orders` at their own pace, and a new consumer can start from the beginning to rebuild its state. This "many readers, replayable" behaviour is the heart of the difference between a log and a traditional queue.

### A topic is a set of partitions

A topic with N partitions is N independent logs numbered 0 to N-1. Each has its own offsets, so offset 5 in partition 0 and offset 5 in partition 2 are unrelated records. Kafka places each partition on a broker (its **leader**) and copies it to other brokers for safety, as the chapter on replication explains. A partition is never split across brokers.

blocks.text: A partition is the unit of five different things, and it helps to keep them apart when you reason about Kafka.

rows: Kafka keeps records in order inside a partition. It makes no promise about order between partitions.

In a consumer group each partition is read by at most one member at a time (share groups, described later, are the exception), so the partition count is the ceiling for consumer parallelism. Producers also write to partitions in parallel.
A partition is a directory of files on a broker's disk. It cannot grow beyond what the leader's disks can hold, and spreading partitions evenly is how a cluster balances load.
Every partition has its own leader, its own followers and its own set of in-sync replicas.
When a broker fails, every partition it led needs a new leader. More partitions means more elections and more recovery work.
blocks.caption: A partition is the unit of five different things.

blocks.text:
### Which partition does a record go to?

The producer decides, and it follows this order:

1. If the record names a partition explicitly (`new ProducerRecord<>(topic, partition, key, value)`), that partition is used.
2. Otherwise, if the record has a key, the partition is `toPositive(murmur2(keyBytes)) % numPartitions`. Murmur2 is a fast, non-cryptographic hash. It is applied to the **serialized** key bytes, and `toPositive` clears the sign bit so that the result is never negative.
3. Otherwise (no key) the producer's built-in logic spreads records across partitions. It is *sticky*: it keeps using one partition until about one batch worth of data (`batch.size`) has gone to it and then switches, because a few large batches are cheaper than many tiny ones. With the default `partitioner.adaptive.partitioning.enable=true` it also sends more records to partitions whose brokers respond faster.

The setting `partitioner.class` is `null` by default, which means "use the built-in logic above". The old `DefaultPartitioner` and `UniformStickyPartitioner` classes were removed in Kafka 4.0; their behaviour is simply built in now. If you want the key to be ignored for partitioning, there is `partitioner.ignore.keys` (default `false`).

Because the hash is computed over bytes, two producers that serialize the "same" key differently (say, one as plain text and one as JSON) send it to different partitions. Clients in other programming languages may also use a different default hash function. If a topic is written by more than one kind of client, check that they agree.

The listing below computes the partition for a few ShopStream order ids with Kafka's own hash function, once for three partitions and once for four.

blocks.title: WhichPartition.java

blocks.code:
o-1001  3 partitions -> 1   4 partitions -> 1
o-1002  3 partitions -> 1   4 partitions -> 3
o-1003  3 partitions -> 2   4 partitions -> 3
o-1004  3 partitions -> 2   4 partitions -> 1

Going from three to four partitions moved five of the six keys. That is typical rather than unlucky. For a uniform hash, a key keeps its partition when the count goes from N to N+1 with probability only 1/(N+1). The next section shows why that matters.

### Adding partitions: what changes and what breaks

You can increase the partition count of a topic but never decrease it; the documentation says plainly that Kafka does not support reducing the number of partitions.

blocks.title: Increase the partition count of orders from 3 to 6

blocks.text:
Adding partitions does not move any existing record. Old records stay in their old partitions, and only new records are routed with the new count. For a keyed topic this has consequences:

- **Per-key ordering breaks across the change.** Order `o-1003` had its history in partition 2. After the change its next event may go to partition 5, and a different consumer instance will process it, possibly before the old partition's backlog has been handled. For a short time the events of one order can be processed out of order.
- **Compacted topics keep stale copies.** Compaction works inside one partition. The old value of a key stays in the old partition forever (nothing newer arrives there to replace it), while the new value lives in the new partition. A reader that merges all partitions into a table may see two values for one key.
- **Stateful consumers lose their locality.** A Kafka Streams state store, a local cache or a per-partition aggregate was built on the assumption that a key always arrives in the same partition. Joins in Kafka Streams also assume that both topics have the same number of partitions.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A consumer that has no committed offset for a newly added partition applies `auto.offset.reset`. With the default `latest` it starts at the end of that partition at the moment it learns about it. Records that producers appended in the gap (producers refresh their metadata, and consumers theirs, at different moments) are skipped. For topics that grow partitions, `earliest` is the safer choice.

The safe approaches are all variations on "decide generously at the start". If you must change the count of a topic whose key ordering matters, stop the producers, let the consumers drain the topic, add partitions, and restart. Or create a new topic with the desired count, copy or dual-write into it, and move the consumers over. Both are projects, not one-liners.

### How many partitions?

There is no magic number, but there is a reasoned way to choose. Start from three questions.

1. **Throughput.** How much data per second must the topic absorb at peak? Measure what one partition sustains on your hardware (the producer and consumer performance tools in the CLI toolbox exist for this) and divide.
2. **Consumer parallelism.** A consumer group cannot use more consumers than there are partitions, so the partition count must be at least the largest number of consumer instances you will want to run. Measure what one consumer instance can process, including your own business logic, and divide the target throughput by it.
3. **Growth and key distribution.** Because the count cannot be changed freely later, size for the load you expect in a year or two, not for today. Prefer numbers with many divisors, such as 6, 12 or 24, so that 2, 3, 4 or 6 consumers share the partitions evenly.

**The sizing rule of thumb**

blocks.code:
partitions  ≥  max( T / p ,  T / c )      then add headroom, then round to a friendly number

T = peak throughput the topic must handle
p = throughput one partition sustains for producers   (measure it)
c = throughput one consumer instance can process      (measure it, with your real logic)

blocks.text:
An illustrative example (made-up numbers, not a benchmark): ShopStream's `page-views` topic must absorb 10 MB/s at peak. Measurements say one partition accepts 20 MB/s of writes, but one consumer instance, doing real work per event, processes only 2 MB/s. Producers need 10/20, so one partition; consumers need 10/2 = 5. Take 5, double it for growth, round to 12. The consumers set the answer, not Kafka's write speed. The `orders` topic is the opposite case: it carries little data, so throughput alone would say one partition, but you may want up to six `payment-service` instances for availability and rolling deployments, so 6 is chosen for parallelism.

More partitions are not free. Every partition adds costs that grow with the count:

- Each replica of each partition is a directory with several open files per segment (log, offset index and time index) on a broker.
- Followers must fetch every partition they replicate, so replication work and the number of small requests grow.
- When a broker fails, all the partitions it led need new leaders, and when it comes back each one must be recovered and caught up.
- Cluster metadata, which every broker and client keeps and refreshes, grows with the partition count.
- Clients hold memory per partition: the producer keeps a batch per partition and the consumer buffers fetched data per partition.

KRaft (described in the next chapters) raised the number of partitions a cluster can manage compared with the ZooKeeper era, but it did not make partitions free. The production chapters on capacity planning give sizing guidance.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not create 1000 partitions "to be safe". Over-partitioning wastes memory and file handles, slows recovery after failures, and still cannot be undone, since partitions can never be removed. Pick a reasoned number, measure, and grow when the numbers say so.

### Ordering, stated precisely

What exactly does Kafka guarantee about order?

- Records that one producer sends to one partition are appended in the order they were sent. With the idempotent producer (the default in Kafka 4.x), retries cannot reorder them.
- A consumer reads a partition in offset order.
- Therefore all records with the same key are read in the order they were produced, as long as they went to the same partition, which means as long as the partition count stayed the same.
- There is no order between partitions, between topics, or between two producers writing to the same partition at the same time (the order in which their batches reach the leader decides).

In ShopStream the topics `orders`, `payments`, `inventory` and `shipments` all use `orderId` as the key, so the events of one order are ordered within each topic. The `StockReserved` event of an order is still not ordered relative to its `PaymentAuthorized` event, because they are in different topics. Services must be written to cope with that, which is what the saga and state-machine patterns in the Part on design patterns are about.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: A topic has 6 partitions and you start 10 consumers in the same group. What happens, and how do you keep events of one customer in order? Six consumers each get one partition and the other four sit idle: a group's parallelism is capped by the partition count. To keep one customer's events in order, use the customer id as the record key. The same key always hashes to the same partition, one consumer reads that partition, and offsets within it are strictly increasing. The guarantee holds only while the partition count is unchanged.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A topic is a set of independent append-only logs (partitions). Offsets are per partition, never reused, and (topic, partition, offset) identifies a record.
- The partition is the unit of ordering, parallelism, storage placement, replication and failure. Kafka orders records only within a partition.
- A keyed record goes to `murmur2(keyBytes) % numPartitions` (made positive); keyless records are spread by the producer's sticky, adaptive logic.
- Adding partitions never moves old data but re-routes new keys, which breaks per-key ordering, compaction assumptions and partition-local state. Partitions cannot be removed.
- Choose the count from measured throughput, the largest consumer count you will need and expected growth, then round to a number with many divisors.

sections.title: Records, Batches and the Wire Format

blocks.text:
When you call `send()` you think about one record: a key, a value, maybe a header or two. Kafka does not move or store records one at a time. Producers group records into **batches**, brokers append whole batches to the log, and consumers fetch whole batches back. Understanding the record and the batch explains several things that otherwise look odd: why compression is configured on the producer, why a "message size limit" is really a batch size limit, why offsets sometimes skip a number, and why a producer waits a few milliseconds before sending.

### What a record contains

A record has the parts below. The topic and partition say where it lives; everything else is the record itself.

rows: Optional bytes. Decides the partition (when none is given) and the identity of the record for log compaction. Null means "no key".
Optional bytes: your payload. A null value is a **tombstone**: in a compacted topic it means "delete this key".
Zero or more pairs of a String name and an optional byte array, for metadata such as an event type, a trace id or a content type. Names may repeat. Headers do not affect partitioning.
Milliseconds since the epoch. Which clock is used depends on the topic's timestamp type (below).
The record's position in its partition, assigned when it is appended. The producer cannot choose it.
blocks.caption: The parts of a record.

blocks.text:
Kafka never looks inside the key or the value. They are opaque byte arrays, and turning objects into bytes (and back) is the job of serializers, covered in the Part on serialization and schemas.

### From records to record batches

Sending one record per network request would waste almost everything: the request header, a round trip, a checksum, an index update. So the producer collects records headed for the same partition into a **batch** and sends the batch as one unit. (The accumulator that does this is described in the Part on the Java producer; `batch.size` and `linger.ms` control it.) The batch is also the unit that the broker validates, appends and replicates, and that consumers fetch. If a consumer asks to start at offset 1 and offsets 0 to 2 live in one batch, the broker returns the whole batch and the client discards the records before offset 1.

Since version 0.11 Kafka has used one on-disk and on-the-wire format, called **magic v2** (the "magic byte" is the format version, and its value is 2). Kafka 4.0 removed support for the two older formats. A v2 batch looks like this:

**Record batch layout (magic = 2)**

blocks.code:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ baseOffset            int64   offset of the first record in the batch        │
│ batchLength           int32   number of bytes after this field               │
│ partitionLeaderEpoch  int32   stamped by the leader when it appends          │
│ magic                 int8    format version (2)                             │
│ crc                   uint32  CRC-32C of everything from attributes on       │
├───────────────────────────── covered by the CRC ─────────────────────────────┤
│ attributes            int16   compression, timestamp type, txn, control      │
│ lastOffsetDelta       int32   offset of the last record minus baseOffset     │
│ baseTimestamp         int64   timestamp of the first record                  │
│ maxTimestamp          int64   largest timestamp in the batch                 │
│ producerId            int64   -1 if the producer is not idempotent           │
│ producerEpoch         int16   used to fence old producers                    │
│ baseSequence          int32   sequence number of the first record            │
│ recordsCount          int32   number of records                              │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ records (if compressed, this whole part is one compressed block)             │
│   each record: length, attributes, timestampDelta, offsetDelta,              │
│                key length + key, value length + value, headers               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

blocks.text:
The fixed header adds up to 61 bytes per batch (8+4+4+1+4+2+4+8+8+8+2+4+4), no matter how many records the batch holds. That is the main saving of batching: the per-record cost is only a few bytes of lengths and deltas. Four details are worth remembering.

- **Deltas keep records small.** Each record stores its offset and timestamp as a (variable-length) difference from `baseOffset` and `baseTimestamp`, so consecutive records cost a byte or two for each.
- **Producer fields enable idempotence.** `producerId`, `producerEpoch` and `baseSequence` let the broker detect duplicates and fence zombie producers. The chapter on delivery semantics builds on them.
- **The leader epoch tells replicas which "era" wrote the data.** The partition leader stamps `partitionLeaderEpoch` when it appends. The field sits before the checksum and is not covered by it, so the broker can set it without recomputing the CRC. The chapter on replication shows how epochs are used to find and remove diverging data after a leader change.
- **The attributes field packs flags.** The table below lists them.

Control batch (a transaction marker, never shown to applications)
The base timestamp field holds the delete horizon (used by log compaction)
blocks.caption: The attributes field of a batch (16 bits).

blocks.text:
A **control batch** holds a single control record: a commit or abort marker written when a transaction finishes. Consumers use it to filter out aborted data and never hand it to your code. But it does occupy an offset, so in a topic written with transactions you will see gaps of one offset where markers sit. Never assume that two consecutive records you receive have consecutive offsets.

### Compression works on batches

Compression is set on the producer with `compression.type`: `none` (the default), `gzip`, `snappy`, `lz4` or `zstd`. The records of a batch are compressed together as one block, which is why batching and compression reinforce each other: a larger batch holds more similar-looking records (the same JSON field names over and over) and compresses better. The batch header stays uncompressed so the broker can read offsets, timestamps and producer fields without decompressing anything.

The broker has a topic setting, also called `compression.type`, whose default is `producer`. It means "keep whatever codec the producer used", so the broker can store the batch as it arrived and later serve it to consumers and followers unchanged. The consumer decompresses it. If you force a topic to a different codec from the one producers use, the broker must decompress and recompress every batch, which costs CPU on the busiest machines in your cluster. The sensible split is: choose the codec on the producer (the Part on the Java producer discusses the trade-offs between the four codecs) and leave the topic on `producer`.

### Timestamps: CreateTime and LogAppendTime

Every record carries a timestamp. Which clock it comes from is a per-topic choice, `message.timestamp.type`:

- **CreateTime** (the default): the timestamp the producer put in the record, normally the time of the `send()` call, or a value you set explicitly. This is event time as seen by the producer.
- **LogAppendTime**: the broker overwrites the timestamp with its own clock when it appends the batch. Use it when you cannot trust the clocks of the producers and you do not need event time.

rows: Which clock fills the timestamp field
How far in the past (compared with the broker's clock) a CreateTime may be before the broker rejects the record
How far in the future a CreateTime may be before the broker rejects the record
blocks.caption: Topic settings that govern timestamps.

blocks.text:
The "after" limit became one hour in Kafka 4.0 (before, it was effectively unlimited), because one producer with a wrong clock could write records stamped far in the future. Timestamps matter more than they seem: time-based retention looks at the timestamps in a segment, the time index behind "give me the offset for this time" lookups is built from them, and Kafka Streams uses them as event time for windows and joins. A bad clock therefore does not just make a record look odd; it can delay deletion and confuse time-based replay.

### Size limits

The size limits all talk about batches, not individual records, and they live in three places.

rows: The size of a produce request and, in effect, of one uncompressed batch. A record that is too large fails on the client with `RecordTooLargeException`.
The largest record batch the broker accepts for this topic, measured after compression. Its default comes from the broker setting `message.max.bytes`.
How much data one fetch returns per partition and in total. They are soft limits (see below).
blocks.caption: Where message size is limited.

blocks.text:
The broker default 1048588 is exactly 1 MiB plus the 12-byte prefix (base offset and length) that precedes every batch. The consumer limits are deliberately soft. If the first batch of the first non-empty partition is larger than the limit, the broker still returns it, so a consumer can always make progress. A limit that is too small therefore slows a consumer down but does not strand it.

To allow larger messages for one topic you raise `max.message.bytes` on that topic and `max.request.size` on the producers that write to it. Before you do, ask whether the payload belongs in Kafka at all. Large messages inflate memory use on producers, brokers and consumers, delay everything queued behind them in the same partition, and make every fetch heavier. The claim-check pattern in the Part on design patterns (store the file elsewhere, send a reference) is usually the better answer.

### Looking at a batch on disk

You can inspect real batches with the dump tool. The sample below shows one batch holding three `orders` records that were stored in partition 1. (The partition was chosen by the key hash as in the previous chapter: both `o-1001` and `o-1002` map to partition 1 of a three-partition topic.) The numbers are examples; the real tool prints each batch on a single long line, wrapped here to fit the page. The lab on looking inside the log in the hands-on Part shows how to find the right file.

blocks.text: What to notice: the three records share one batch header, so `baseOffset` is 0 and `lastOffset` is 2. The batch is 263 bytes in total, which is the 61-byte header plus the three small records. The batch `CreateTime` is the largest timestamp of the batch, and each record carries its own. `producerId` and the `sequence` numbers show that the producer was idempotent (the default); a producer with idempotence turned off would show -1 there. `compresscodec: none` means the producer did not compress.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Is compression applied per message or per batch, and who does the work? Per batch. The producer compresses the records of one batch together, the broker normally stores the batch exactly as it arrived, and the consumer decompresses it. Bigger batches compress better, and because the topic default is `compression.type=producer` the broker avoids recompressing, so compression saves network, disk and replication bandwidth without moving the work onto the brokers. Forcing a different codec on the topic makes the broker recompress, which is usually a mistake.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Kafka stores and moves record batches, not single records. The batch is the unit of compression, checksum, append, replication and fetch.
- A v2 batch has a fixed 61-byte header (base offset, timestamps, producer id, epoch, sequence, attributes, CRC-32C) followed by delta-encoded records.
- Compression is chosen by the producer and covers a whole batch; with the topic default `producer` the broker keeps the batch as received.
- CreateTime is the producer's clock and LogAppendTime the broker's. Retention, time-based offset lookups and Streams event time all depend on timestamps.
- Size limits apply to batches and exist on the producer, the topic and the consumer. Prefer small messages and the claim-check pattern to raising limits.

A Kafka cluster is a group of **brokers**: JVM processes that store partitions and answer produce and fetch requests. But someone also has to hold the cluster's *metadata*: which topics exist, how many partitions each has, which brokers hold their replicas, who leads each partition, which brokers are alive, what the configs and ACLs are. Whoever holds that truth takes every important decision, so it must be consistent and must survive failures. For its first decade Kafka kept the metadata in a separate system, Apache ZooKeeper. Since Kafka 4.0 there is no ZooKeeper. Kafka stores its metadata in its own replicated log and keeps that log consistent with its own implementation of the Raft consensus protocol. This mode is called **KRaft** (Kafka Raft), and it is the only mode in the 4.x line.

### The metadata log

In KRaft the cluster metadata is an event log, just like application data. It lives in an internal single-partition log named `__cluster_metadata`. Every change to the cluster is a record appended to it: a topic is created, a partition gets a new leader, a broker registers, a config changes, a feature level is raised. The current state of the cluster is simply the result of replaying that log from the beginning (or from a snapshot, below). It is not an ordinary topic: clients cannot read or write it, and it is replicated by the Raft protocol of the controller quorum rather than by the ISR mechanism described in the next chapter.

Every Kafka process is a **node** with a unique `node.id`, and the setting `process.roles` decides what it does.

blocks.text:
In a production cluster you run dedicated controller nodes (three or five of them) next to the brokers. Controllers do little work and need few resources; the KRaft documentation says that about 5 GB of memory and 5 GB of disk for the metadata log is sufficient for a typical cluster.

### The controller quorum

The controller nodes form a **quorum**. One of them is the leader, called the **active controller**; the others are followers (standby controllers) that keep a copy of the metadata log. The protocol is Raft, in a variant adapted to Kafka:

- **Epochs and elections.** Every period of leadership has a number, the *epoch* (Raft calls it a term). A follower that does not hear from the leader for a short time (a few seconds at most, governed by the `controller.quorum.*` timeouts) becomes a candidate, asks the other voters for their votes in a new, higher epoch, and becomes leader if a majority agrees. A higher epoch always wins, so an old leader that comes back cannot cause damage.
- **Majority commit.** The leader appends a record to its own log; followers fetch it (pull, using the same Fetch request that ordinary replication uses). A record is **committed** when a majority of the voters have stored it, and only committed records are applied to the cluster state. A committed record survives any failure that leaves a majority alive, because at least one surviving voter has it.
- **One decision maker.** Only the active controller makes decisions. It processes admin requests (create a topic, change a config), notices that a broker has failed, picks new partition leaders, and writes the resulting records. Because the standby controllers already hold the log, taking over is just an election, not a reload of the cluster state from an external system.

blocks.text:
**How many controllers?** A quorum of 2N+1 voters tolerates N failures, because a majority (N+1) must remain. Three controllers survive one failure, five survive two. Even numbers do not help: four voters need three for a majority and still tolerate only one failure, so you pay for a node you do not benefit from. Going beyond five rarely makes sense, since every metadata change waits for a majority and metadata changes are small and infrequent anyway.

**Static or dynamic membership.** Every node sets `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers`, a list of controller endpoints that it uses to find the quorum. This is the dynamic quorum (KIP-853): controllers can be added with `bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh add-controller` and removed with `remove-controller`, and the documentation advises removing a controller from the quorum before you shut it down for good. The older static quorum lists every voter, with id, host and port, in `controller.quorum.voters`; its membership cannot change at runtime. The kind of quorum is decided when the storage is formatted (the hands-on Part shows the commands for a three-node cluster), and a feature level `kraft.version` of 1 or higher means dynamic.

### How brokers use the metadata

Brokers are observers of the metadata log. Each broker fetches `__cluster_metadata` from the active controller, applies the records to an in-memory copy of the cluster state, and also keeps the log on disk (in `metadata.log.dir`, which defaults to the first entry of `log.dirs`). That has three useful consequences.

- **Clients talk to brokers only.** A producer or consumer asks any broker for metadata and gets the answer from that broker's in-memory copy: for each partition the leader, the replicas and the leader epoch, plus the broker endpoints. Clients never contact controllers.
- **Restarts are quick.** A broker that restarts loads its latest snapshot and replays only the log after it.
- **Propagation is simple.** Instead of the controller pushing updates to every broker, as it did in the ZooKeeper era, every broker pulls the same log and ends in the same state.

A **snapshot** is a file with the complete metadata state at one offset of the log. Each node writes snapshots periodically, which lets it delete the log before the snapshot. A new or far-behind node can fetch a snapshot instead of replaying months of history. Snapshot files end in `.checkpoint`.

blocks.text:
### Broker lifecycle: registration, heartbeats and fencing

How does the cluster know which brokers are alive without ZooKeeper sessions? Through registration and heartbeats.

1. A starting broker contacts the controller quorum (using `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers`) and **registers**: it announces its `node.id`, a fresh incarnation id, its listeners and the feature levels it supports. If this does not succeed within `initial.broker.registration.timeout.ms` (default 60000) the broker process exits.
2. A newly registered broker is **fenced**. It has not yet caught up on the metadata log, so it must not lead partitions. It fetches the log while sending heartbeats that tell the controller how far it has got.
3. When the broker has caught up, the active controller **unfences** it. It can now lead partitions and serve clients.
4. The broker keeps sending heartbeats every `broker.heartbeat.interval.ms` (default 2000). If the controller hears nothing for `broker.session.timeout.ms` (default 9000), it fences the broker again: the broker is removed from the in-sync replica sets of its partitions, and new leaders are elected for the partitions it led.

**Controlled shutdown** uses the same channel. When you stop a broker normally (`kafka-server-stop.sh` sends SIGTERM), the broker tells the controller it wants to shut down, the controller first moves partition leadership to other replicas, and only then does the broker stop. Clients see a short, orderly leader change instead of waiting for a session timeout. It is on by default (`controlled.shutdown.enable=true`).

rows: Nothing visible. The quorum still has a majority (2 of 3), so metadata changes continue. Replace the node at leisure.

The remaining controllers elect a new leader, typically within seconds. Brokers keep serving produce and fetch requests on their existing leaders, but metadata changes and new leader elections wait until the election is over.

No metadata change can be committed: no new topics, no leader elections, no broker registrations. Brokers can usually keep serving the partitions they already lead, but the cluster cannot react to the next failure. Restoring a majority of controllers resumes normal operation.
The controller fences it after missed heartbeats and elects new leaders for its partitions from their in-sync replicas (see the next chapter).

All `zookeeper.*` settings are gone, and so is `kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper`: tools talk to the cluster with `--bootstrap-server` (or `--bootstrap-controller` for tools that address a controller directly). Policy plug-ins such as `CreateTopicPolicy` now run in the controllers, so their jars must be on the controllers' class path.

### Looking at the quorum

The tool `kafka-metadata-quorum.sh` shows who leads the metadata quorum and how far behind the others are. The values below are examples; after the summary the real output lists every controller (the voters) and every broker (the observers) with their ids and directory ids.

blocks.text: Three more tools help when you want to look inside. `kafka-dump-log.sh` with `--cluster-metadata-decoder` decodes the segments and snapshots of the metadata directory into readable records. `kafka-metadata-shell.sh` opens a snapshot and lets you browse the cluster state with commands such as `ls` and `cat`. And `kafka-features.sh describe` shows the feature levels, including `metadata.version`, which replaces the old `inter.broker.protocol.version` and is how a cluster is moved to new capabilities after an upgrade.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why did Kafka drop ZooKeeper, and what replaced it? ZooKeeper was a second distributed system to deploy, secure, monitor and scale, and the metadata it held limited how many partitions a cluster could manage, because after a controller failover the new controller had to load all the state from ZooKeeper. KRaft stores the metadata in an internal log (`__cluster_metadata`) replicated by a Raft quorum of controller nodes. Standby controllers already hold the state, brokers keep up by fetching the log, and failover is an election instead of a reload. The result is one system to operate and faster recovery with more partitions.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Kafka 4.x runs on KRaft only. Cluster metadata is the `__cluster_metadata` log, replicated by a quorum of controllers using Raft (epochs, majority commit, snapshots).
- `process.roles` is `broker`, `controller` or both. Use three (or five) dedicated controllers in production; 2N+1 controllers tolerate N failures.
- Brokers are non-voting observers: they fetch and replay the metadata log and answer client metadata requests from memory. Clients never talk to controllers.
- A broker registers, starts fenced, is unfenced when caught up, and is fenced again if heartbeats stop for `broker.session.timeout.ms` (9 s). Controlled shutdown moves leaders away before the broker stops.
- Losing the controller majority freezes metadata changes (no elections, no topic creation) but does not by itself stop brokers from serving the partitions they lead.

sections.title: Replication: Leaders, Followers and the ISR

blocks.text:
Disks fail, machines reboot and racks lose power. A partition that lives on one broker disappears together with that broker. Kafka therefore keeps several copies of every partition, called **replicas**, on different brokers. The number of copies is the **replication factor** (RF), and RF 3 is the normal choice for data you care about. Replication is what lets a cluster lose a broker and carry on. It also raises the questions this chapter answers: which copy is in charge, when is a write "safe", and what happens to the data on a copy that was left behind.

### Leaders and followers

For each partition exactly one replica is the **leader** and the others are **followers**. All writes go to the leader, and normally all reads do too (the section on reading from followers shows the exception). The ordered list of a partition's replicas is printed as `Replicas` by `kafka-topics.sh --describe`; its first entry is the **preferred leader**. Kafka assigns replicas round-robin so that every broker leads a fair share of the partitions. After failures have scrambled the leadership, `auto.leader.rebalance.enable` (default `true`) lets the controller move leaders back to their preferred replicas; it checks every `leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds` (default 300).

blocks.text:
Followers **pull**. A follower runs fetcher threads that send Fetch requests to the leader, exactly like a consumer, and append the returned batches unchanged to their own log. Because the batch bytes are copied as they are, a follower's log has the same offsets as the leader's. Fetch requests long-poll: the leader holds one until `replica.fetch.min.bytes` (default 1) of data is available or `replica.fetch.wait.max.ms` (default 500) has passed. `num.replica.fetchers` (default 1) sets the number of fetcher threads per source broker. Pull replication has pleasant properties: the leader keeps no per-follower push state, a slow follower slows only itself, and replication uses the same fast path (page cache, zero copy) as consumers.

### Log end offset, high watermark and committed records

Three terms describe the state of replication, and they come up in every discussion of Kafka's guarantees.

- The **log end offset (LEO)** of a replica is the offset that the next record appended to its log will get. Every replica has its own LEO.
- The **high watermark (HW)** is the offset below which every in-sync replica (next section) has the data. The leader computes it as the smallest LEO among the in-sync replicas.
- A record is **committed** when it lies below the HW. Consumers are only allowed to read committed records. **high watermark: consumers read only below this**

blocks.text:
How does the leader know the followers' LEOs? From the fetch requests themselves: a follower that asks for offset 7 is saying "I have everything below 7". The leader updates its view and advances the HW. It passes the HW back to the followers in its fetch responses, so a follower learns of a new HW one fetch round later than the leader does.

Why hide uncommitted records from consumers? Because a record that is not on every in-sync replica could vanish if the leader failed right now. If consumers could read it, two consumers might disagree about history after a failover. The HW guarantees that anything a consumer has seen will still exist after the leader changes.

A consumer has two positions of its own. Its **position** is the offset of the next record it will fetch. Its **committed offset** is the last position it saved to Kafka (in `__consumer_offsets`) as a bookmark for restarts. The distance between the end of the visible log and the consumer's position is the **lag**.

### The in-sync replicas (ISR)

Which followers should the HW wait for? Not all of them: one dead follower would freeze every write. Kafka waits for the **in-sync replicas (ISR)**. The documentation defines an in-sync replica by two conditions: it keeps an active session with the controller, so it receives metadata updates, and, if it is a follower, it replicates the leader's writes and does not fall "too far" behind. The leader is always a member of the ISR.

"Too far behind" is measured in time, not in messages. The leader removes a follower from the ISR if it has not fetched, or not caught up to the leader's log end offset, within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (default 30000). The follower is added back once it has caught up. A broker that the controller fences (missed heartbeats, see the previous chapter) is removed from the ISRs sooner, after `broker.session.timeout.ms` (default 9000). ISR changes are committed through the controller (a leader asks for them with an `AlterPartition` request), so the ISR is part of the cluster metadata, which is why `describe` can show it.

The documentation states the consequence: a write is not considered committed until all in-sync replicas have received it, and with f+1 replicas a topic can tolerate f failures without losing committed messages. Compare that with a majority-vote scheme, which needs 2f+1 replicas for the same tolerance. That economy is the reason Kafka uses an ISR.

### acks and min.insync.replicas

The producer's `acks` setting decides when the leader answers, and the topic setting `min.insync.replicas` sets a floor on how small the ISR may be before the leader refuses to answer at all.

blocks.text: `all` is the default in Kafka 4.x. But it means all *in-sync* replicas, and the ISR can shrink to the leader alone. The guard is `min.insync.replicas` (default 1): when `acks=all` and the ISR has fewer members than this, the leader rejects the write with `NotEnoughReplicasException` rather than accept a write that is protected by too few copies. The documentation notes that the setting takes effect only when the producer uses `acks=all`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: With the default `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all` is only as safe as `acks=1` whenever the ISR has shrunk to the leader. The producer gets an acknowledgement for data that exists on one machine.

The standard recipe for data you cannot afford to lose is RF 3, `min.insync.replicas=2`, producers with `acks=all`, and `unclean.leader.election.enable=false` (its default). A record is then acknowledged only when at least two brokers hold it, so any single failure leaves a copy; writes continue while two replicas remain in sync; and the cluster refuses writes instead of quietly lowering the protection. In general such a topic tolerates `min.insync.replicas - 1` simultaneous failures without losing acknowledged data, and `RF - min.insync.replicas` failures without losing the ability to write.

### Leader election and leader epochs

When the controller finds that a leader has failed or been fenced, it elects one of the remaining ISR members as the new leader. Every ISR member holds all committed records, so an election never loses committed data.

Each period of leadership is numbered by a **leader epoch**, which grows by one at every change. The leader stamps the epoch into each batch it appends (the `partitionLeaderEpoch` field from the chapter on batches), and each replica keeps a small `leader-epoch-checkpoint` file recording the first offset of each epoch. Epochs solve a subtle problem. After a failover a replica may hold records that the new leader never received. They were not committed, or the new leader would have them, but they occupy offsets that the new leader will soon reuse for different records. The returning replica must find the point where its log diverges and cut it off. It asks the leader, with an `OffsetForLeaderEpoch` request, "where did my last epoch end in your log?" and truncates to that offset before it resumes fetching. (Older Kafka versions truncated to the high watermark instead, which in rare failure sequences left different records at the same offset on different replicas.)

Clients benefit from epochs as well. Requests carry the epoch the client knows, so a broker that has stopped being the leader recognises a stale request and rejects it. The client then refreshes its metadata and retries on the new leader.

### Three failures, step by step

The scenarios use the `orders` topic with RF 3, `min.insync.replicas=2`, an idempotent producer with `acks=all`, and the defaults for timeouts.

#### Scenario 1: a follower crashes

Broker 1 leads a partition, broker 3 is a follower, and the ISR is {1,2,3}. **Timeline of scenario 1**

blocks.code:
t0  steady state       ISR {1,2,3}; all three replicas have offsets up to 100; HW 100
t1  broker 3 crashes   ISR is still {1,2,3}. The leader keeps appending (LEO 120) but the
                       HW stays at 100, so acks=all produce requests wait for broker 3
t2  about 9 s later    the controller misses broker 3's heartbeats, fences it and removes it
                       from the ISR: ISR {1,2}, HW jumps to 120, waiting requests complete
t3  degraded service   ISR size 2 ≥ min.insync.replicas 2, so writes keep succeeding. The
                       partition is under-replicated (UnderReplicatedPartitions = 1)
t4  broker 3 restarts  it re-registers, catches up on metadata, checks against the leader's
                       epoch history that its log is a prefix of the leader's, and fetches
                       the 20 missing records
t5  caught up          the leader asks for broker 3 to rejoin the ISR: ISR {1,2,3}

If broker 3 had not crashed but merely stalled while still heartbeating, the controller would not fence it; the leader would drop it after `replica.lag.time.max.ms`, so the pause could last up to 30 seconds. #### Scenario 2: the leader crashes with unreplicated records

This is the case that explains HW, epochs and idempotence at once. Broker 1 leads in epoch 0. The letters stand for records; `X` and `Y` are two recent records (in two separate batches) that the producer sent and has not yet seen acknowledged.

**Timeline of scenario 2**

blocks.code:
offset:                          0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
t0  broker 1 (leader, epoch 0)  [A A A A A A X Y]  LEO 8
    broker 2 (follower)         [A A A A A A X  ]  LEO 7
    broker 3 (follower)         [A A A A A A    ]  LEO 6   HW = 6, so only A is committed
t1  broker 1 crashes. The controller elects broker 2 from the ISR; epoch 1 begins.
t2  The producer's requests fail. It refreshes its metadata and resends X and Y to broker 2
    with the same producer id and sequence numbers:
      X is already in broker 2's log: recognised as a duplicate, not appended again
      Y is new to broker 2: appended at offset 7 (epoch 1), call it Y'
    broker 2 (leader, epoch 1)  [A A A A A A X Y']  LEO 8
    broker 3 (follower)         [A A A A A A X Y']  after fetching; HW = 8, acks sent
t3  broker 1 restarts as a follower. Its log is [A A A A A A X Y] and its Y is from epoch 0.
    It asks broker 2: "where did epoch 0 end?"  Answer: offset 7.
    Broker 1 truncates its log to offset 7, then fetches Y' and joins the ISR again.

blocks.text:
What was lost? Nothing that had been acknowledged: X and Y were never acknowledged, so the producer retried them. Other settings would have gone differently. With `acks=1`, broker 1 would have acknowledged Y on its own, and after the crash Y would be gone for good although the producer believes it was stored. Without idempotence, the retry of X would be appended a second time and stored twice. Three mechanisms cooperate here: `acks=all` prevents loss, the idempotent producer prevents duplicates, and leader epochs keep the replica logs identical.

#### Scenario 3: both followers fall behind

Now both followers become unreachable (a network partition, or two brokers down) while broker 1 stays up.

**Timeline of scenario 3**

blocks.code:
t0  steady state       ISR {1,2,3}, min.insync.replicas = 2: writes succeed
t1  brokers 2 and 3    after the controller fences them (about 9 s) or the leader drops them
    unreachable        (30 s of lag), the ISR is {1}
t2  producers          acks=all and ISR size 1 < 2: the leader answers NotEnoughReplicasException.
                       The producer retries until delivery.timeout.ms (120 s), then the send
                       fails with a TimeoutException. Consumers still read below the HW.
t3a broker 2 returns   it catches up and rejoins the ISR: ISR {1,2}; writes resume, nothing lost
t3b broker 1 now fails no in-sync replica is alive. With unclean.leader.election.enable=false
    too (worst case)   the partition goes offline until a safe replica is back (broker 1, or
                       with ELR a replica that left the ISR below the minimum): no data
                       lost, but no availability either

blocks.text:
This is the availability-versus-consistency decision in concrete form. With the default `min.insync.replicas=1` the leader would have kept accepting `acks=all` writes at t2 into an ISR of one, and the failure at t3b would have destroyed those writes. With `min.insync.replicas=2` it refuses them, and the producer sees errors instead of silently weaker durability.

### Unclean leader election and eligible leader replicas

What if no in-sync replica is alive? The documentation names the two options. Wait for an ISR member to return (consistency over availability), or elect any replica that is alive, even one that is missing committed records (availability over consistency). The second is an *unclean* leader election. The topic and broker setting `unclean.leader.election.enable` chooses, and its default has been `false` since version 0.11, so Kafka waits. Turning it on means accepting that records can vanish and that offsets can be reused by different records. It can be reasonable for data such as metrics or logs where uptime matters more than completeness. For orders and payments it is the wrong choice.

**Eligible leader replicas (ELR, KIP-966)** narrow the gap between the two options. Under the "strict min ISR" rule, once the ISR falls below `min.insync.replicas` the high watermark can no longer advance, so nothing new can be committed. The replicas that were in the ISR at that moment therefore still hold every committed record even after they drop out of it. The controller remembers them as the partition's ELR. When it needs a leader it chooses from the ISR first, then from the ELR (a member that is not fenced), and only then falls back to the last known leader. ELR arrived in Kafka 4.0 and is enabled by default on new clusters from 4.1 (the feature level `eligible.leader.replicas.version`). One visible consequence is that `min.insync.replicas` becomes a cluster-level setting rather than a per-broker one, and changing it clears the ELR state. In daily work the rule is unchanged: set `min.insync.replicas` deliberately and leave unclean election off.

### Reading from followers

By default every fetch goes to the leader. When clients and brokers sit in different availability zones, that can mean a lot of cross-zone traffic, which cloud providers often bill. Since Kafka 2.4 (KIP-392) a consumer can read from a follower in its own rack. You enable it with `broker.rack` on each broker, the broker setting `replica.selector.class=org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector`, and `client.rack` on the consumer (the documentation says it corresponds with the broker's `broker.rack`). The leader answers the consumer's fetch with the preferred replica, and the consumer fetches from there. The data is still limited to the high watermark, which a follower learns slightly later than the leader, so records can appear to such a consumer a little later in exchange for cheaper traffic.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the ISR, and why does Kafka not simply wait for all replicas? The ISR is the set of replicas, leader included, that are alive and have caught up within `replica.lag.time.max.ms`. A write is committed when every ISR member has it, and new leaders are chosen only from the ISR, so committed data survives. Waiting for all replicas would let a single dead or slow follower stall every write. Waiting for a majority, as Raft does, would need 2f+1 replicas to tolerate f failures, while the ISR design needs f+1. The price is that the ISR can shrink, which is why `min.insync.replicas` exists.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What happens when a partition leader dies? The controller notices (missed heartbeats, or a controlled shutdown), elects a new leader from the ISR and increases the leader epoch. Clients get a not-leader error, refresh their metadata and retry against the new leader. Committed records are safe because every ISR member has them. Records that only the old leader held were never acknowledged under `acks=all`, so the producer retries them, and idempotence prevents duplicates. When the old leader returns it truncates its log using the epoch history and becomes a follower. If no ISR member is alive the partition stays offline, unless unclean election is enabled.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Each partition has one leader and RF-1 followers that pull from it. A follower's log is a byte-for-byte copy with the same offsets.
- The high watermark is the smallest log end offset among the in-sync replicas. Only records below it are committed and visible to consumers.
- The ISR contains the replicas that are alive and caught up (`replica.lag.time.max.ms`, 30 s). With f+1 replicas, f failures lose no committed data. New leaders come from the ISR.
- `acks=all` plus `min.insync.replicas=2` with RF 3 plus `unclean.leader.election.enable=false` is the durable recipe. With `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all` can degrade to leader-only safety.
- Leader epochs let a returning replica find and truncate diverging records. Unclean election and ELR govern what happens when the ISR is gone.
